claim: Ventral visual stream neural responses are dynamic, even for static image presentations.
source: Ventral visual stream neural responses are dynamic, even for static image presentations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that motivates the study.

claim: Approximately 30 milliseconds after the initially evoked response, neurons in intermediate level areas decreased their responses to typical configurations of their preferred face parts relative to their response for atypical configurations.
source: Remarkably,~30 milliseconds after the initially evoked response, we found that neurons in intermediate level areas decreased their responses to typical configurations of their preferred face parts relative to their response for atypical configurations even while neurons in higher areas achieved and maintained a preference for typical configurations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons in higher areas achieved and maintained a preference for typical configurations while intermediate areas showed decreased preference.
source: Remarkably,~30 milliseconds after the initially evoked response, we found that neurons in intermediate level areas decreased their responses to typical configurations of their preferred face parts relative to their response for atypical configurations even while neurons in higher areas achieved and maintained a preference for typical configurations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data comparing different hierarchical stages.

claim: The hierarchical neural dynamics were inconsistent with standard feedforward circuits.
source: These hierarchical neural dynamics were inconsistent with standard feedforward circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing observed data to computational models.

claim: Recurrent models computing prediction errors between stages captured the observed temporal signatures.
source: Rather, recurrent models computing prediction errors between stages captured the observed temporal signatures.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results that fit the neural data.

claim: Neural responses to static images may encode top-down prediction errors in addition to bottom-up feature estimates.
source: This model of neural dynamics, which simply augments the standard feedforward model of online vision, suggests that neural responses to static images may encode top-down prediction errors in addition to bottom-up feature estimates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The primate ventral visual stream is a hierarchically organized set of cortical areas beginning with the primary visual cortex (V1) and culminating with distributed patterns of neural firing across the inferior temporal cortex (IT).
source: The primate ventral visual stream is a hierarchically organized set of cortical areas beginning with the primary visual cortex (V1) and culminating with distributed patterns of neural firing across the inferior temporal cortex (IT) that explicitly encode objects (i.e. linearly decodable object identity) (Hung et al., 2005) and quantitatively account for core invariant object discrimination behavior in primates (Majaj et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IT neural firing patterns explicitly encode objects in a linearly decodable manner.
source: The primate ventral visual stream is a hierarchically organized set of cortical areas beginning with the primary visual cortex (V1) and culminating with distributed patterns of neural firing across the inferior temporal cortex (IT) that explicitly encode objects (i.e. linearly decodable object identity) (Hung et al., 2005) and quantitatively account for core invariant object discrimination behavior in primates (Majaj et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hung et al., 2005.

claim: IT neural patterns quantitatively account for core invariant object discrimination behavior in primates.
source: The primate ventral visual stream is a hierarchically organized set of cortical areas beginning with the primary visual cortex (V1) and culminating with distributed patterns of neural firing across the inferior temporal cortex (IT) that explicitly encode objects (i.e. linearly decodable object identity) (Hung et al., 2005) and quantitatively account for core invariant object discrimination behavior in primates (Majaj et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Majaj et al., 2015.

claim: Feedforward models achieve impressive performance in object categorization similar to the absolute level of performance achieved by IT neural populations.
source: Formalizing object recognition as the result of a series of feedforward computations yields models that achieve impressive performance in object categorization (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) similar to the absolute level of performance achieved by IT neural populations, and these models are the current best predictors of neural responses in IT cortex and its primary input layer, V4 (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on deep learning models.

claim: Feedforward models are the current best predictors of neural responses in IT cortex and V4.
source: Formalizing object recognition as the result of a series of feedforward computations yields models that achieve impressive performance in object categorization (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) similar to the absolute level of performance achieved by IT neural populations, and these models are the current best predictors of neural responses in IT cortex and its primary input layer, V4 (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cadieu et al., 2014 and Yamins et al., 2014.

claim: IT neural responses are well-known to be dynamic even in response to images without dynamic content.
source: However, visual object recognition behavior may not be executed via a single feedforward neural processing pass (a.k.a. feedforward inference) because IT neural responses are well-known to be dynamic even in response to images without dynamic content (Brincat and Connor, 2006; Sugase et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014), raising the question of what computations those neural activity dynamics might reflect.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The three face processing subregions (pIT, cIT, aIT) are tightly anatomically and functionally connected.
source: First, prior evidence argues that these three face processing subregions are tightly anatomically and functionally connected and that the subregion in pIT is the dominant input to the higher subregions (Grimaldi et al., 2016; Moeller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The subregion in pIT is the dominant input to the higher subregions (cIT and aIT).
source: First, prior evidence argues that these three face processing subregions are tightly anatomically and functionally connected and that the subregion in pIT is the dominant input to the higher subregions (Grimaldi et al., 2016; Moeller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: In aIT, neurons rapidly developed and maintained a response preference for the typical frontal configuration of the face parts.
source: Consistent with the idea that the overall system performs – among other things -- face vs non-face discrimination (i.e. face detection), we found that in the highest face processing stage (aIT), neurons rapidly developed and maintained a response preference for the typical frontal configuration of the face parts even though our images were designed to be challenging for frontal face detection.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Many neurons in pIT and cIT showed an overall stronger response for atypical face-part configurations relative to typical face-part configurations over time.
source: However, we found that many neurons in the early (pIT) and intermediate (cIT) processing levels of IT paradoxically showed an overall stronger response for atypical face-part configurations relative to typical face-part configurations over time.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Neurons in pIT and cIT evolved an apparent preference for images of misarranged face parts within 30 milliseconds of their feedforward response.
source: That is, these neurons evolved an apparent preference for images of misarranged face parts within 30 milliseconds of their feedforward response.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Standard feedforward models that employ local recurrences such as adaptation, lateral inhibition, and normalization could not capture the stage-wise pattern of image selectivity.
source: We found that standard feedforward models that employ local recurrences such as adaptation, lateral inhibition, and normalization could not capture this stage-wise pattern of image selectivity despite our best attempts.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results.

claim: A decreasing relative preference for typical face-part configurations in early and intermediate processing stages is a natural dynamical signature of error coding models.
source: However, we found that a decreasing -- rather than increasing – relative preference for typical face-part configurations in early and intermediate processing stages is a natural dynamical signature of previously suggested 'error coding' models (Rao and Ballard, 1999) in which the neural spiking activity at each processing stage carries both an explicit representation of the variables of interest (e.g. Is an eye present? And is a whole face present?) and an explicit encoding of errors computed between each pair of stages in the hierarchy (e.g. a face was present, but the eye was not present at the correct location).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results and comparison to prior theoretical work.

claim: 115 pIT sites, 70 cIT sites, and 40 aIT sites were tested with the face versus non-face challenge set.
source: Results are reported here for sites that were spatially located in a face-selective subregion, that showed visual drive to any category in the screen set (see Materials and methods), and that were subsequently tested with our face versus non-face challenge set (Figure 1B, left panel) (n = 115 pIT, 70 cIT, and 40 aIT sites).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample size.

claim: 21 images drove the mean, early (60–100 ms) pIT population response to > 90% of its response to the intact face.
source: This procedure generated both frontal face and non-face arrangements of the face parts, and we identified 21 images (red and black boxes) that drove the mean, early (60–100 ms) pIT population response to > 90% of its response to the intact face (first image in red box is synthesized whole face; compare to the second image which is the original whole face), and of these 21 images, 13 images contained atypical, non-face arrangements of the face parts.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Of the 21 pIT-matched images, 13 images contained atypical, non-face arrangements of the face parts.
source: This procedure generated both frontal face and non-face arrangements of the face parts, and we identified 21 images (red and black boxes) that drove the mean, early (60–100 ms) pIT population response to > 90% of its response to the intact face (first image in red box is synthesized whole face; compare to the second image which is the original whole face), and of these 21 images, 13 images contained atypical, non-face arrangements of the face parts.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Population decoding classification accuracy for typical vs atypical face-part configurations was near chance level (50%) in pIT.
source: However, we found that population decoding classification accuracy for the pIT-matched typical vs atypical face-part configurations we used here was near chance level (50%) in pIT (Figure 1C, blue bar; by comparison, classification accuracy for face versus non-face objects classification was 99.6% using the same pIT sites).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Linear population decoding classification of typical vs atypical face-part configurations was well above chance in cIT and aIT.
source: Further downstream in regions cIT and aIT, we found that the linear population decoding classification of these early pIT response-matched typical vs atypical face-part configurations was well above chance, suggesting that our pIT-matched face-part configuration detection challenge is largely solved somewhere between pIT and aIT (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 66% of pIT sites responded more strongly to atypical over typical face-part configurations in the late response phase (100–130 ms).
source: A late response modulation for atypical over typical face-part configurations was not restricted to the example sites as a majority of pIT sites (66%) responded more strongly to atypical over typical face-part configurations in the late response phase (prefer typical frontal face-part arrangement: 60–90 ms = 66% vs 100–130 ms = 34%; p = 0.000, n = 115) (Figure 3B, blue bars) even though almost all sites preferred faces over non-face objects throughout this time-course (60–90 ms = 98% vs 100–130 ms = 90%; p = 0.009, n = 115).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Almost all pIT sites preferred faces over non-face objects throughout the time-course (60–90 ms = 98% vs 100–130 ms = 90%).
source: A late response modulation for atypical over typical face-part configurations was not restricted to the example sites as a majority of pIT sites (66%) responded more strongly to atypical over typical face-part configurations in the late response phase (prefer typical frontal face-part arrangement: 60–90 ms = 66% vs 100–130 ms = 34%; p = 0.000, n = 115) (Figure 3B, blue bars) even though almost all sites preferred faces over non-face objects throughout this time-course (60–90 ms = 98% vs 100–130 ms = 90%; p = 0.009, n = 115).
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Of the 51 pIT sites that showed a significantly changing preference for typical face-part configurations over time, 84% showed a decreasing preference.
source: Of the 51 sites in our pIT sample that showed a significantly changing preference for typical face-part configurations over time (p < 0.01 criterion for significant change in d'), 84% of these sites showed a decreasing preference (n = 43 of 51 sites, p < 10^−6, binomial test, n = 115 total sites) (Figure 3A, left column, light gray vs black lines).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The decreasing trend for typical face-part configurations was observed in both monkeys when analyzed separately.
source: This surprising trend -- decreasing relative response for typical face-part configurations versus atypical face-part configurations -- was observed in both monkeys when analyzed separately (pM1 = 0.000, pM2 = 0.002, nM1 = 43, nM2 = 72 sites; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Responses to face images with normally arranged face parts were weaker by 18% on average in the late phase compared to the early phase.
source: Responses to these images were weaker by 18% on average in the late phase of the response compared to the early phase (Δrate (60–90 vs 100–130 ms) = −18% ± 4%, p = 0.000; n = 7 images) while responses to the images with atypical spatial arrangements of face parts -- also capable of driving high early phase responses -- did not experience any firing rate reduction in the late phase of the response (Δrate (60–90 vs 100–130 ms) = 2 ± 1%, p = 0.467; n = 13 images).
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Responses to images with atypical spatial arrangements of face parts did not experience any firing rate reduction in the late phase of the response.
source: Responses to these images were weaker by 18% on average in the late phase of the response compared to the early phase (Δrate (60–90 vs 100–130 ms) = −18% ± 4%, p = 0.000; n = 7 images) while responses to the images with atypical spatial arrangements of face parts -- also capable of driving high early phase responses -- did not experience any firing rate reduction in the late phase of the response (Δrate (60–90 vs 100–130 ms) = 2 ± 1%, p = 0.467; n = 13 images).
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The relative speed of the decreasing preference for typical face-part configurations (starting 30 milliseconds after response onset) argues against arousal or attention mechanisms.
source: The relative speed of this decreasing preference for typical face-part configurations – starting 30 milliseconds after response onset – argues against arousal or attention mechanisms as those phenomena occur over long timescales, and our stimuli were randomized to avoid top-down priming effects for typical or atypical images.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of the observed effects and knowledge about attention mechanisms.

claim: When initial responses were tightly matched site-by-site, a significant drop in preference for images with typical frontal face-part arrangements versus atypical face-part arrangements was still observed in pIT.
source: This image selection procedure virtually eliminated any differences in initial responses between the images of typical and atypical face-part configurations and hence any firing rate difference driven by potential differences in nuisance parameters when rearranging the face parts (Figures 3C and 60–90 ms), yet we still observed a significant drop in preference for images with typical frontal face-part arrangements versus atypical face-part arrangements in pIT (Δd' = −0.10 ± 0.03, p = 0.001, n = 77) (Figure 3C, blue line).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The pattern of late phase population firing rates in pIT across images could not be significantly predicted from early phase pIT firing rates for each image.
source: Further arguing against this activity-dependent hypothesis, we found that the pattern of late phase population firing rates in pIT across images could not be significantly predicted from early phase pIT firing rates for each image (ρpIT early, pIT late = 0.07 ± 0.17, p = 0.347; n = 20 images).
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis.

claim: When controlling for the number of face parts, pIT face selectivity still decreased for one, two, and four part image subsets.
source: When we recomputed selectivity across subsets of images containing a matched number of one, two, or four parts (n = 5, 30, and 3 images, respectively), we still observed that pIT face selectivity decreased. For all three image subsets controlling the number of face parts, d' of the pIT population began positive on average in the sampled pIT population (i.e. preferred frontal face-part arrangements in 60–90 ms post-image onset) (median d' for 60–90 ms = 0.13 ± 0.05, 0.05 ± 0.02, 0.33 ± 0.09 for one, two, and four parts) and significantly decreased in the next phase of the response (100–130 ms post-image onset) becoming negative on average (median d' for 100–130 ms: −0.27 ± 0.06,–0.14 ± 0.02,–0.04 ± 0.12; one, two, four parts: p = 0.000, 0.000, 0.004, for d' comparisons between 60–90 ms and 100–130 ms, n = 115, 115, 76 sites) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A similar decreasing face-part configuration selectivity profile was observed when single part images were re-tested at smaller (3°) and larger (12°) image sizes.
source: A similar decreasing face-part configuration selectivity profile was observed when we re-tested single part images at smaller (3o) and larger (12o) image sizes suggesting a dependence on the relative configuration of the parts and not on their absolute retinal location or absolute retinal size (median d' for 60–90 ms vs 100–130 ms: three degrees = 0.51 ± 0.09 vs −0.29 ± 0.14, twelve degrees = 0.07 ± 0.14 vs −0.11 ± 0.14; n = 15; p = 0.000, 0.025, 0.07) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 98% of aIT sites did not significantly change their relative preference for typical versus atypical configurations of the face parts from their initial feedforward response.
source: Also, in contrast to the dynamic selectivity profiles observed in many pIT sites, 98% of aIT sites (39 of 40) did not significantly change their relative preference for typical versus atypical configurations of the face parts from their initial feedforward response (p < 0.01 criterion for significant change at the site level) (Figure 3A, right column, bottom row, dark gray sites).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A stable selectivity profile over time was observed in aIT (median d': 60–90 ms = 0.13 ± 0.03 vs 100–130 ms = 0.17 ± 0.03, p = 0.34, n = 40 sites).
source: Rather, we observed a stable selectivity profile over time in aIT (median d': 60–90 ms = 0.13 ± 0.03 vs 100–130 ms = 0.17 ± 0.03, p = 0.34, n = 40 sites).
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The majority of anterior sites preferred images with typical frontal configurations of the face parts in the late phase of the response (78% of sites).
source: As a result, the majority of anterior sites preferred images with typical frontal configurations of the face parts in the late phase of the response (prefer typical face-part configuration: 60–90 ms = 78% of sites vs 100–130 ms = 78% of sites; p = 0.451, n = 40 sites; Figure 3B, red bars) despite only a minority (34%) of upstream sites in pIT preferring these images in their late response.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Early response patterns in cIT and aIT were significant predictors of late phase activity in pIT.
source: Interestingly, we found that the turning profiles across images in the early response phases of cIT and aIT were significant predictors of late phase activity in pIT (ρcIT early, pIT late = -0.52 ± 0.11, p = 0.000; ρaIT early, pIT late = -0.36 ± 0.14, p = 0.012; npIT = 115, ncIT = 70, naIT = 40 sites; n = 20 images), even better predictors than early phase activity in pIT itself (ρpIT early, pIT late = 0.07 ± 0.17, p = 0.347).
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis.

claim: For images that produced high early phase responses in cIT and aIT, the following later phase responses of units in pIT tended to be low.
source: That is, for images that produced high early phase responses in cIT and aIT, the following later phase responses of units in the lower level area (pIT) tended to be low, consistent with error coding models which posit that feedback from higher areas (in the form of predictions of the face features) would contribute to the decreasing activity observed in lower areas encoding those face features.
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis and interpreted in the context of error coding models.

claim: The face-selective subregions in IT are connected forming an anterior to posterior hierarchy and pIT serves as the primary input into this hierarchy.
source: Previous functional and anatomical data show that the face-selective subregions in IT are connected forming an anterior to posterior hierarchy and show that pIT serves as the primary input into this hierarchy (Moeller et al., 2008; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Grimaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The dynamics of error signals in the hierarchical model naturally displayed a strong decrease of selectivity in a sub-component of its first processing stage.
source: We found that the dynamics of error signals in our hierarchical model naturally displayed a strong decrease of selectivity in a sub-component of its first processing stage -- qualitatively similar behavior to the selectivity decrease that we observed in many pIT and cIT neural sites (Figure 5A, second column, blue and green curves).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All feature coding control models failed to reproduce the observed neural dynamics across the ventral visual hierarchy.
source: However, all of these state coding control models failed to reproduce the observed neural dynamics across the ventral visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results.

claim: The selectivity of feature coding models simply increased to a saturation level set by the leak term in the system.
source: Rather, the selectivity of these models simply increased to a saturation level set by the leak term (shunting inhibition) in the system as in the strictly feedforward model (Figure 5A, first column).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The population preference for normally configured face parts in the intermediate processing stages decreases over time.
source: We have measured neural responses during a difficult discrimination between images with typical and atypical face-part configurations across the IT hierarchy and demonstrated that the population preference for normally configured face parts in the intermediate (a.k.a hidden) processing stages decreases over time – that is population responses at lower levels of the hierarchy (pIT and cIT) signal deviations of their preferred features from their expected configuration whereas the top level (aIT) rapidly developed and then maintained a preference for natural, frontal face-part configurations.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary experimental findings.

claim: Population responses at lower levels of the hierarchy (pIT and cIT) signal deviations of their preferred features from their expected configuration.
source: We have measured neural responses during a difficult discrimination between images with typical and atypical face-part configurations across the IT hierarchy and demonstrated that the population preference for normally configured face parts in the intermediate (a.k.a hidden) processing stages decreases over time – that is population responses at lower levels of the hierarchy (pIT and cIT) signal deviations of their preferred features from their expected configuration whereas the top level (aIT) rapidly developed and then maintained a preference for natural, frontal face-part configurations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The top level (aIT) rapidly developed and then maintained a preference for natural, frontal face-part configurations.
source: We have measured neural responses during a difficult discrimination between images with typical and atypical face-part configurations across the IT hierarchy and demonstrated that the population preference for normally configured face parts in the intermediate (a.k.a hidden) processing stages decreases over time – that is population responses at lower levels of the hierarchy (pIT and cIT) signal deviations of their preferred features from their expected configuration whereas the top level (aIT) rapidly developed and then maintained a preference for natural, frontal face-part configurations.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The relative speed of selectivity changes in pIT makes high-level explanations based on fixational eye movements or shifts in attention unlikely.
source: The relative speed of selectivity changes in pIT makes high-level explanations based on fixational eye movements or shifts in attention (e.g. from behavioral surprise to unnatural arrangements of face parts) unlikely as saccades and attention shifts occur on slower timescales (hundreds of milliseconds) (Egeth and Yantis, 1997; Müller et al., 1998; Ward et al., 1996) than the ~30 ms dynamical phenomena we observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of the observed effects and knowledge about eye movements and attention, supported by citations.

claim: The presence of stronger responses to typical than to atypical face-part configuration images in aIT argues against general arousal effects.
source: The presence of stronger responses to typical than to atypical face-part configuration images in aIT further argues against general arousal effects which would have predicted stronger not weaker responses to surprising, atypical images in aIT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and expectations from arousal mechanisms.

claim: The rapid propagation of neural signals over tens of milliseconds suggested intracortical processing within the ventral visual stream in a manner that was not entirely consistent with a pure feedforward model.
source: Rather, the rapid propagation of neural signals over tens of milliseconds suggested intracortical processing within the ventral visual stream in a manner that was not entirely consistent with a pure feedforward model, even when we included strong nonlinearities in these models such as normalization and even when we stacked these operations to form more complex three stage models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and computational modeling results.

claim: Augmenting the feedforward model so that it represented the prediction errors generated during hierarchical processing of atypical configurations produced the observed neural dynamics and hierarchical pattern of signal propagation.
source: However, augmenting the feedforward model so that it represented the prediction errors generated during hierarchical processing of atypical configurations produced the observed neural dynamics and hierarchical pattern of signal propagation (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: Many IT neurons code error signals.
source: This view argues that many IT neurons code error signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The exact mechanism for producing prediction errors remains to be determined.
source: However, the exact mechanism for producing prediction errors remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: Multiple visual neurophysiology studies have shown evidence of neural responses consistent with error signals.
source: Multiple visual neurophysiology studies have shown evidence of neural responses consistent with error signals. This includes the seminal predictive coding study on end-stopping in V1 (Rao and Ballard, 1999). More recently, studies in IT have used pairing of images over time to create sequences with predictable temporal structure and found evidence of putative error signals when those statistically exposed temporal predictions were violated (Meyer et al., 2014; Schwiedrzik and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The present work revealed error coding dynamics that are naturally present in the system without using statistical exposure or behavioral training to induce signals.
source: Our work expands those IT findings in three directions. First, we revealed error coding dynamics that are naturally present in the system without using statistical exposure or behavioral training to induce signals.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present work compared to prior studies.

claim: Errors in the present study depended on the spatial statistics of the features rather than depending on temporal statistics.
source: Second, errors depended on the spatial statistics of the features -- rather than depending on temporal statistics -- which may be more directly related to native, spatial form processing in IT.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present work compared to prior studies.

claim: The present work identified a putative source of face prediction signals in downstream IT by recording from multiple areas in the same experiment.
source: Third and perhaps most importantly, we identified a putative source of face prediction signals in downstream IT by recording from multiple areas in the same experiment and showing that early signals in anterior areas were (negatively) correlated with late signals in pIT.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present work compared to prior studies.

claim: Early signals in anterior areas were negatively correlated with late signals in pIT.
source: Third and perhaps most importantly, we identified a putative source of face prediction signals in downstream IT by recording from multiple areas in the same experiment and showing that early signals in anterior areas were (negatively) correlated with late signals in pIT.
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis.

claim: The pattern of observed dynamics in pIT, cIT, and aIT were difficult to account for quantitatively when using feature coding models but could be computationally modeled at a population level using a simple error coding model.
source: Formalizing this claim, we found that the pattern of observed dynamics in pIT, cIT, and aIT were indeed difficult to account for quantitatively when using feature coding models but could be computationally modeled at a population level using a simple error coding model (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The suggestion that many IT neurons code errors is consistent with the observation of strong responses to extremes in face space.
source: Our suggestion that many IT neurons code errors is consistent with the observation of strong responses to extremes in face space (Leopold et al., 2006) providing an alternative interpretation to the prior suggestion that cIT neurons are not tuned for typical faces but are instead tuned for atypical face features (i.e. extreme feature tuning) (Freiwald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the present findings to prior observations, supported by citations.

claim: Some IT neurons are preferentially tuned to typical spatial arrangements of face features, and other IT neurons are involved in coding errors with respect to those typical arrangements.
source: Under the present hypothesis, some IT neurons are preferentially tuned to typical spatial arrangements of face features, and other IT neurons are involved in coding errors with respect to those typical arrangements.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The multi-stage neural dynamics observed in the data could not be adequately fit by only using lateral recurrences such as adaptation, lateral inhibition, and standard forms of normalization.
source: Crucially, we found that the multi-stage neural dynamics observed in our data could not be adequately fit by only using lateral recurrences such as adaptation, lateral inhibition, and standard forms of normalization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stimuli were specifically chosen to evoke similar levels of within stage neural activity to limit the effects of known mechanisms that depend on activity levels through lateral interactions.
source: Indeed, we specifically chose our stimuli to evoke similar levels of within stage neural activity to limit the effects of known mechanisms that depend on activity levels through lateral interactions (e.g. adaptation, normalization), and we fully expect that these activity dependent mechanisms would operate in parallel to top-down, recurrent processes during general visual processing.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: The present study provides evidence that errors are not only computed, but that they might be explicitly encoded in spiking rates.
source: The present study provides evidence that errors are not only computed, but that they might be explicitly encoded in spiking rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The result at the level of population neural dynamics was robust across choices of cost function.
source: We emphasize that this result at the level of population neural dynamics was robust across choices of cost function; we tested models with different unsupervised and supervised performance errors (reconstruction, nonlinear reconstruction, and discriminative) and found similar population level error signals across these networks (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Errors provide control signals for guiding learning giving error-computing networks additional adaptive power over basic feature estimation networks.
source: In error-computing networks, errors provide control signals for guiding learning giving these networks additional adaptive power over basic feature estimation networks.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the computational utility of error signals.

claim: Observation of error signals may provide insight into how more intelligent unsupervised and supervised learning algorithms such as backpropagation could be plausibly implemented in the brain.
source: Observation of error signals may provide insight into how more intelligent unsupervised and supervised learning algorithms such as backpropagation could be plausibly implemented in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings.

claim: Gradient descent algorithms are facilitated by using an error code so that efficient learning is reduced to a simple Hebbian operation at synapses and efficient inference is simply integration of inputs at the cell body.
source: A potentially important contribution of this work is the suggestion that gradient descent algorithms are facilitated by using an error code so that efficient learning is reduced to a simple Hebbian operation at synapses and efficient inference is simply integration of inputs at the cell body (see Equation 10 and text in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the computational utility of error coding, supported by the model equations.

claim: Two rhesus macaque monkeys weighing 6 kg (Monkey 1, female) and 7 kg (Monkey 2, male) were used.
source: Two rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) weighing 6 kg (Monkey 1, female) and 7 kg (Monkey 2, male) were used.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Multi-unit activity (MUA) was systematically recorded at 300 micron intervals starting from penetration of the superior temporal sulcus.
source: Multi-unit activity (MUA) was systematically recorded at 300 micron intervals starting from penetration of the superior temporal sulcus such that all sites at these regular intervals were tested with a screen set containing both faces and non-face objects, and a subset of sites that were visually driven were further tested with our main image set manipulating the position of face parts.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Previous work showed similar responses between single-units and multi-units on images of the type presented here.
source: Although we did not record single-unit activity, our previous work showed similar responses between single-units and multi-units on images of the type presented here (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012), and our results are consistent with observations in previous single-unit work in IT (Freiwald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The visual response latencies in monkey two were on average 13 ms slower than those in monkey one for corresponding face-selective regions.
source: Finally, given that the visual response latencies in monkey two were on average 13 ms slower than those in monkey one for corresponding face-selective regions, we applied a single latency correction (13 ms shift to align monkey 1 and monkey 2's data) prior to averaging across monkeys.
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis.

claim: There was <10 ms average latency difference between pIT, cIT, and aIT.
source: Furthermore, there was <10 ms average latency difference between pIT, cIT, and aIT so that a common 30 ms wide analysis window for early (60–90 ms) and late (100–130 ms) firing rates was sufficient across IT stages.
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis.
